patterns.title: Escalation
patterns.domain: Systems and feedback traps; reciprocal intensification, relative goals, perception and response delays, and structural restraint

sources.title: Daniel H. Kim, Escalation: The Underlying Structure of War (September 1999)
sources.supports: Named systems archetype, locally corrective but mutually amplifying actions, relative perceptions, action/perception delays, and altered competition or response rules.
sources.read_method: Full web article opened and read: opening/relative-position framing, both delays, reinforcing diagram explanation, escalating response stages, and early-warning/intervention discussion. Original PDF was returned in indexed full text with byline and September 1999 imprint, but its subsequent direct fetch was throttled; direct reading claims rely on the full web text.
sources.boundary: Conceptual/practitioner synthesis, not a theorem that every response escalates or an empirical estimate of the hypothetical arms race. Corporate anecdotes, historical arms-race claims, and fictional WarGames conclusions are not imported as verified case evidence or guidance.

sources.title: Donella H. Meadows, Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008; linked UK edition 2009), edited by Diana Wright
sources.supports: Relative goals, reciprocal intensification, reinforcing structure, unilateral restraint, and negotiated controlling rules.
sources.read_method: Chapter five's Escalation section, printed pages 124–126 (PDF pages 140–142), opened and read through trap/way-out statements, including short-run advantage and negotiated controls. Publication/edition information was checked earlier in this collection's research.
sources.boundary: Conceptual account and practical recommendations, not proof of inevitable exponential growth or collapse. An earlier numerical example used an additive rule with linear growth. The current qualitative article specifies no numerical response rule and predicts no particular rate of increase. Dated international, business, medical-cost, and cultural examples are not imported as current empirical facts.

sources.title: Sukhwinder S. Shergill, Paul M. Bays, Chris D. Frith, and Daniel M. Wolpert, Two Eyes for an Eye: The Neuroscience of Force Escalation (2003)
sources.supports: A specific laboratory demonstration of force amplification under instructions to match and evidence concerning self-generated versus externally generated sensation.
sources.read_method: Original published one-page Science paper opened and read in full: six-pair alternating force task, separate twelve-person direct-versus-joystick matching task, instructions, findings, sensory-attenuation interpretation, and methodological limits. PubMed record opened to verify authors, date, DOI, and Science 301:187. Author-lab publication listing was also opened for identity corroboration.
sources.boundary: Small sensorimotor study, not evidence of governments’ threat interpretation, general intergroup conflict, aggression motives, universal escalation rates, or effectiveness of this article's practical interventions. No paper effect size is transferred to the hypothetical arms-race example.

sources.title: Barry M. Staw, Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy: A Study of Escalating Commitment to a Chosen Course of Action (1976)
sources.supports: Definition and historical research context for escalation of commitment, a different mechanism that can operate without reciprocal rivalry.
sources.read_method: Original eighteen-page published scan opened; abstract, self-justification/investment framing, alternative-mechanism qualifications, and student-role-play method read directly. Publisher record checked for publication identity and DOI.
sources.boundary: Used only to distinguish neighboring terminology. No universal effect, current replication claim, broad irrationality diagnosis, or exact estimate from this experiment is asserted. This is not presented as a full-paper results audit.

patterns.short_description: Trace how each side's corrective action becomes the other's reason to intensify, then change the response rule or the conditions that make restraint costly.
use_when: How does one response become the other side’s next threat?
Hypothetical Eastland and Westland respond to each other’s perceived arms buildup.
goals: Recognize the familiar predicament before specialist terminology.
Explain the defining mechanism and distinguish neighboring concepts.

Causal hypothesis, not a documented historical attribution. Procurement is a pipeline; deliveries add and retirement removes equipment. Other threats, unequal power, noncompliance, budgets, and delays can alter the response.
Separate hypothetical behavior, model results, documented cases, and practical editorial proposals.
mechanisms: Negotiate defined reciprocal limits covering stock and pending deliveries, with credible verification and a breach process.
Verification costs resources; breach, other threats, and unequal power can prevent restraint or make it costly.
example_user_queries: How does one response become the other side’s next threat?

visual.question: How does one response become the other side’s next threat?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. Eastland’s perceived shortfall prompts arms procurement, which contributes to Westland’s perceived threat and procurement, feeding Eastland’s concern. Orders await delivery; deliveries and retirements change arms held. A proposed reciprocal limit includes pending deliveries and credible verification. Change: Replace automatic matching with defined, observable reciprocal limits where feasible. Limitation: Verification costs resources; breach, other threats, and unequal power can prevent restraint or make it costly.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. The loop is a hypothetical causal account of reciprocal pressure, not evidence about a historical arms race. Verified limits change the response relationship only if definitions, observation, and compliance work. An order pause does not retire existing equipment or guarantee security.
